target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Ran the full replay at 1.26M events/sec end-to-end on an order book that keeps std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map to make cancels O(1)
bullet_feedback.problem: Breaks the structure rule: 'Ran ... at 1.26M events/sec' is a measurement, not 'did X to accomplish Y', and the data-structure description is tacked on as a second idea. 'std::list FIFOs per price level in a std::map with an order-ID hash map' is a three-container noun stack nobody says aloud. The throughput number has no baseline or hardware context, and std::list is a well-known cache-unfriendly choice that a performance-minded interviewer will challenge immediately.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The page's main 'performance-sensitive systems' claim rests on a number the reader cannot judge and a design the reader may consider a weakness, so it can backfire in a systems interview.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 1.26M events/sec is compared against (single thread? what machine?) and why the cancel path mattered
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the design choice and its purpose in one sentence, then attach the throughput as the result, e.g. 'Kept a hash map from order ID to each resting order so cancels run in O(1), which let the full replay run at 1.26M events/sec'. Be ready to defend std::list or drop the container names.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick robot grasps that avoid hitting the table for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR
bullet_feedback.problem: Tacks an extra clause onto the end ('for a PhD-led project targeting ICLR'), which violates the one-clause structure rule. 'targeting ICLR' reads as a venue claim for unsubmitted work. There is no outcome: the bullet ends at intent ('to help ... pick').
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader skims 'ICLR' and assumes a paper, then feels misled when asked; and with no result, the bullet shows activity rather than a working system.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the overlay measurably changed grasp choices, or say it is in progress
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut the trailing project/venue clause (move 'PhD-led' context to the role line if needed) and end on what the pipeline does for the robot.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill’s main search tool
bullet_feedback.problem: Two problems. Mechanism: it is unclear how precomputing keeps lookups within 'permission' limits (rate limits make sense; permissions do not). Grammar: 'which became the Claude skill's main search tool' grammatically attaches to 'limits', not to the tree, and is an extra clause tacked on at the end.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer will ask 'what permission limit?' and the candidate needs a crisp answer; a recruiter re-reads the sentence to find what 'which' refers to.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the permission constraint was (e.g., read-only replica access, query quota)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint plainly and put the 'main search tool' fact earlier so 'which' has an unambiguous referent, e.g. 'Built the Claude skill's main search tool by caching popular workflows from a 270K-row PostgreSQL table in Redis, so lookups stayed within the database's rate limits'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: Noun stacks: 'EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check' and 'production Amazon Bedrock classifier'. 'its grades' is ambiguous (the judge's grades or the classifier's?), and it is unclear whether the classifier or the check triggers fine-tuning. No result is given.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A non-engineer cannot restate this, and an engineer has to parse it twice to work out the control loop, which is the interesting part.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whose grades drift and what the check compares against
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say the loop in plain order: a scheduled job has a second LLM re-grade the classifier's outputs and kicks off fine-tuning only when the two disagree past a threshold. Keep 'Bedrock' or 'EventBridge', not both, in the sentence.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo’s public-policy staff which research topics are popular
bullet_feedback.problem: 'Co-built' leaves ownership unclear: what did Amar build versus the team? 'deployed it to dev' honestly admits it never reached production, but then the bullet's purpose ('to show ... staff') reads as if it is in use. 'on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK' is a tech dump of three tools with no engineering decision attached.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Ambiguous ownership plus a list of deploy tools is a pattern screeners read as keyword padding; an interviewer will ask 'which part was yours?'.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part Amar owned (the scoring logic, the infra, the deploy pipeline)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name Amar's piece first and keep only the tool that explains it (e.g., if he wrote the infra-as-code, say 'Wrote the AWS CDK stack and CI pipeline that deploy...'); let Skills carry the rest.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga’s Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: The only number (20,000+ visits) measures the product's traffic, not the caching, so the bullet borrows a metric for work it does not measure. 'reduce database load and latency' ends at intent. 'Tortuga' is an unexplained proper noun and 'Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries' is a possessive noun stack.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptical reader sees the metric and the action are unrelated and starts doubting other numbers on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what Tortuga is (the scheduler itself?) and whether the cache's effect was observed at all
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Introduce the product first and frame the traffic as context, e.g. 'Added a Redis cache in front of the database for Tortuga, a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, ...'; drop 'Prisma ORM' from the sentence.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
bullet_feedback.problem: Parenthetical-style tech dump of five names (React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow, Jest) in one stretch. 'make editing smoother' is vague. 'which 90% ... preferred' has no stated comparison (preferred over the legacy tool, presumably) and 'which' attaches to 'editing' rather than the app.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The real story (a visual editor developers chose over the old tool) is buried behind keywords, and the 90% reads as unanchored.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep Electron and the visual editor, cut the rest to Skills, and state the comparison, e.g. '...which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred over the old tool'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
bullet_feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' is a garden-path double object that readers stumble on. 'SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB' plus 'GPT-4o mini' is three named tools in one sentence. 'RAG meal suggestions' is a noun stack.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A recruiter cannot restate what the feature does for a user; the purpose (grounding suggestions in real recipes) is hidden in the tech chain.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say the user-facing behavior first, then the mechanism once, e.g. 'Building meal suggestions for the official UMD app that retrieve real scraped recipes before the LLM answers, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
bullet_feedback.problem: Stacks three metrics in the tail clause. Reports only read-side results; LSM-trees exist to win on writes, so omitting write throughput looks cherry-picked to an informed reader. Why an append-heavy event log needs range queries is not explained.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A storage-literate interviewer will immediately ask 'and writes?'; the bullet invites that question without the page answering it.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: the write-side comparison, or why reads were the deciding workload
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep one headline number and say which backend the engine kept and why, rather than listing three ratios.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
bullet_feedback.problem: 'backtested Java capacity-planning logic' is a noun stack, and 'the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' is a reduced relative clause that reads at first as 'Amazon Redshift reserves' (a noun).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The top-of-page bullet at the strongest brand takes two reads to parse.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add 'that' and unstack, e.g. 'Writing Java logic, checked against historical data, that sets bounds on how much EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift holds back for patching, to balance availability against cost'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of relying on open-ended model search
bullet_feedback.problem: Correct form, but 'instead of relying on open-ended model search' is a tacked-on contrast clause, and 'Claude skill' / 'sub-skills' is insider jargon a recruiter cannot restate.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor length and plain-language cost on an otherwise strong, well-anchored bullet.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Drop the 'instead of...' tail; the contrast is implied by 'focused sub-skills that call ... tools'.

page_feedback.problem: The 'systems-oriented engineer' story only shows up at the bottom (IEX project). The top half is mostly LLM/workflow tooling (Claude skill, LLM-as-judge, RAG, VLM grasps), so a 7-second skim says 'AI-app builder', not 'backend/systems engineer'.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For general backend roles, the strongest systems evidence (Kinesis latency cut, order-book replay accuracy) is not where the eye lands first.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Within each role, put the most backend/systems bullet first (e.g., the Kinesis latency bullet ahead of the topic-scoring tool bullet at Amazon Leo).

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists items no bullet backs up: 'fine-tuning and evaluation', PyTorch, OpenSearch, SQLAlchemy, API Gateway, CloudWatch, psutil.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer who picks one of these and gets a thin answer starts discounting the whole list; 'fine-tuning' in particular overstates a bullet that only triggers fine-tuning.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut skills that cannot be defended for 5 minutes in an interview, or reword 'fine-tuning and evaluation' to match what was actually built (LLM evaluation).

page_feedback.problem: Proper nouns appear with no context: 'Tortuga', 'Amazon Leo', 'AnyGrasp', 'React Flow', 'IEX'.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Each one costs a non-specialist reader a beat, and several stacked in a bullet make it unrestatable.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Give each a 2-3 word gloss the first time it appears (e.g., 'Tortuga, a class scheduler'), or drop it where the generic noun does the job.

page_feedback.problem: Three bullets end at intent with no outcome (AWS capacity bounds, UMIACS grasp pipeline, Bedrock judge check), and four use a trailing 'which ...' clause whose referent is grammatically ambiguous.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The repeated 'which' tail starts to read as a template, which hurts the human-voice impression across the page.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Vary the sentence shapes; use the 'cut <metric> N% by doing X' form where a real number exists and make sure each 'which' sits directly after the noun it describes.

keep: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
Built a C++17 order book and matching engine to replay 50.9M real IEX exchange messages without ever resyncing, which agreed with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices
Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products
Single-column one-page layout with right-aligned dates and sparse bolding
